newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian hackers may have broken Pentagon codes.
newsitem.headline: Croatian hackers may have broken Pentagon codes.

text.p: Three teenage computer hackers in Croatia may have broken Pentagon protection codes and copied highly classified files from United States military bases, according to local media and school officials.
The Zagreb daily Vecernji List said on Wednesday the three high school students, surfing the Internet on their home computer, broke into the database of several U.S. military installations.
The databases included those of the Anderson nuclear installation and an unnamed satellite research centre, it said.
Pentagon officials denied the paper's claim. "There is no way that anybody can tap into classified files via the Internet," Pentagon spokeswoman Lt-Col. Donna Boltz, told Reuters.
Such files are almost always on closed systems without outside access, she said. But hackers trawling the Internet may be able to invade personal E-mail or other sensitive files, she added.
Local reporters flocked to the high school in the Adriatic port of Zadar where the three teenage hackers, aged 15 and 16, specialise in mathematics and information technology.
One of the teenagers, identified only as V.M., told the state news agency HINA he accessed the Pentagon database while surfing the net on January 2.
Despite a warning that he was not allowed to proceed, he continued to browse the site until data from the Anderson base were displayed on the screen, HINA said.
"The data are compressed and need to be extracted, so I don't really know everything they contained, but it sure was very interesting," V.M. told the agency.
He said he was unaware of any possible conseqences.
Assistant Interior Minister Zeljko Sacic told state radio the hackers had broken into the U.S. Defence Department computer system of the airbase on Guam island and several other bases.
The break-in left a trace on the Internet which was tracked down by the Pentagon, reports said.

Vecernji List said the U.S. Defence Department had contacted Croatian police through Interpol to demand an investigation while local police searched the youngsters' flats and confiscated their computer equipment.
The damage caused by the teenagers' destruction of high-profile protection programmes could reach half a million dollars, the daily said.
Computer-hacking is not illegal in Croatia, but the three may be banned for life from accessing the Internet under the current Croatian penal code, the daily Slobodna Dalmacija said.
Police said on Wednesday they were investigating the incident but would not prosecute the youngsters because they were minors.
Zdravko Curko, principal of the Zadar high school the three attend, said they had no criminal intent and their feat was a compliment to their education.

"This is a case of extensive curiosity which had undesired consequences," Curko told Reuters by telephone. "They are excellent students, in love with mathematics and computer science -- they are fanatics in a positive sense of the term."
